svg.text: The two halves reliably learn different things — every single run
The paper’s Figure 3: all 96 first-layer kernels, 11 × 11 × 3, as learned. The split between the two halves, not any individual filter, is the point.
GPU 1, rows 1-3: largely colour-agnostic
GPU 2, rows 4-6: largely colour-specific

g.data-tip: Frequency- and orientation-selective kernels with almost no colour: oriented edges and gratings at several scales. These 48 kernels were learned on GPU 1 and never read a GPU 2 activation.

Colour-specific kernels: coloured blobs and colour-opponent patches, with a few high-frequency gratings. The paper reports this specialisation in every run, independent of the random initialisation, modulo which GPU is which.

a.text: Figure 3 from Krizhevsky et al. 2012 — top three rows GPU 1, bottom three rows GPU 2

What you are meant to see
Not pretty filters. A division of labour
the authors never asked for.
GPU 1 learns frequency- and orientation-
selective kernels with almost no colour.
GPU 2 learns coloured blobs.
The paper reports this specialisation
occurs during every run and does not
depend on the random initialisation,
modulo a renumbering of the GPUs.
Read it as a side effect of the split — the paper never tests whether it helps or hurts
A memory workaround changed what the network learned. Nobody chose to build a colour stream and a shape stream; a 3 GB card did.
The paper is honest that the connectivity pattern is a problem for cross-validation — a hyper-parameter tuned until communication was cheap.
Later background: once cards were big enough nobody rebuilt the asymmetry on purpose; grouped convolution returned as an efficiency device.
